## Today's Goals {.smaller}

Today we will

- Model Assessment and Selection
- Multivariate Modeling in R
  - Implement a model with multiple features
  - Evaluate models
- Team Project Topic Proposal

We will use the CRU **and** FAO data

- `AGNR-AREC280_Fall2026/Data/CRU/parquet`
  - Filter to annual data
- `AGNR-AREC280_Fall2026/Data/FAO/parquet`
  - Filter to Avocado Yields
- Join on `Year` and `ISO3` into a single dataset




  
## Loading Datasets

First load the CRU and FAO data from Parquet Files

```{r load_fao}
#| echo: true
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(arrow)
# Load the full fao dataset
read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"FAO","parquet","FAO_crop_livestock.parquet")
) |>
  filter(Item == "Avocados" & Element == "Yield") -> faostat_avocado

read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"CRU","parquet","tmp_w_ISO3.parquet")
) |>
  filter(Period == "ANN") -> cru_tmp_ann

faostat_avocado |>
  inner_join(cru_tmp_ann,join_by(ISO3,Year),suffix=c("_fao","_cru")) |>
  drop_na(ISO3) -> avocado_tmp
```

## Propose a model

From our visual analysis

- There may be a relationship between temperature and yields
- Propose the linear model
$$Yield = b_0 + b_1 Temperature + \epsilon$$


## Refine our model

From the visual analysis 

- "Baseline" yield varies substantially across countries
  - Reflects the fact that some countries are better suited for avocados
  - At any given temperature yields will be higher
- What if we gave each country it's own "baseline"?
  - Requires a different value of $b_0$ for each country
  
## Factors in R Formulae

You can include **factors** in formulae

- Use the `factor()` function to denote a feature is a factor
- R computes one distinct parameter for **each value** of the factor
  - Distinct values often called **levels**
- Each factor's parameter enters additively when the feature takes on a particular value

## Factors in practice

Suppose you include `factor(ISO3)` in your formula

- R computes a parameter for each value of `ISO3`
  - e.g., `MEX`, `COL`, etc
- Adds the value of the appropriate parameter to the prediction
- e.g.,
  - $Yeild = b_0 + b_1 Temp + b_2^{MEX}$ for Mexico
  - $Yeild = b_0 + b_1 Temp + b_2^{COL}$ for Columbia
- Effectively a new intercept for each `ISO3`

## Example of a factor

Train a model using **only Mexico and Columbia**

```{r train-factor-mex-col}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
library(moderndive)
avocado_tmp |>
  filter(ISO3 %in% c("MEX","COL")) -> avocado_tmp_2cntry

lm(
  Value_fao ~ Value_cru + factor(ISO3),
  data=avocado_tmp_2cntry
) -> yield_model_2ctry

get_regression_table(yield_model_2ctry)
```
Why did I only get one factor parameter?

## Factor Parameter Estimates

You will always get one fewer factor parameter than the number of levels

- All models include an intercept term
- Suppose you compute parameters for each factor level
  - You could subtract 100 from the intercept
  - Add 100 to all factor parameters
  - Exact same predictions
  - Mathematically the same model
  
## Factor Parameter Estimates

You will always get one fewer factor parameter than the number of levels

- If we include all factor parameters in the model
- The intercept would be **colinear** with the factor parameters
- Multiple combinations of values for the intercept and factor parameters give identical predictions
- To solve this R:
  - Chooses one factor level and forces it to be zero (excludes it)
  - The intercept and remaining factor levels are now unique
- R's choice of level to exclude is **arbitrary**
  
  
## A note on Factor Parameter Estimates

R's choice of the *excluded factor level* is arbitrary

- It may not make the same choice each time
- Choosing a different excluded level changes
  - All factor parameters (by the exact same amount)
  - The intercept (by the negative of the factor parameter change)
- Economically 
  - You can only compare factor parameters against each other
  - Comparisons against zero are actually against the excluded level


## Train the model on the full dataset

Model without ISO3 Factors
```{r train-base-all}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
library(moderndive)
lm(
  Value_fao ~ Value_cru + Year,
  data=avocado_tmp
) -> yield_model_base

get_regression_summaries(yield_model_base)
```

Model with ISO3 Factors
```{r train-factor-all}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
lm(
  Value_fao ~ Value_cru + Year + factor(ISO3),
  data=avocado_tmp
) -> yield_model_allctry

get_regression_summaries(yield_model_allctry)
```


## Make a plot

```{r make-plot}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
get_regression_points(yield_model_base) -> points_base
get_regression_points(yield_model_allctry) -> points_allctry

ggplot(data=points_allctry) +
  geom_point(aes(x=Value_fao,y=Value_fao_hat,color=ISO3)) +
  geom_point(data=points_base,aes(x=Value_fao,y=Value_fao_hat), color="#FF00FF",alpha=0.1) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,color="red",linewidth=1.2) +
  labs(
    title="Model Evaluation",
    x="Actual Yield (mt/ha)",
    y="Predicted Yield (mt/ha)",
    color="Country"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_viridis_d()
```

# Feature Interactions

## Interplay between features

The typical linear model assumes the effect of each feature is independent

$$y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_n x_n + \epsilon$$

- The effect of increasing $x_1$ is exactly $b_1$ 
- Regardless of the value of other features

Are there circumstances where this might not hold?

## Feature interactions

The effects of one feature may depend on the value of another feature

- Drought is exacerbated by high temperatures
- Low rain in the current month is moderated by rain in previous months
- High temperatures are bad, but *really high* temperatures are worse

How could we think about accounting for these facts in our models?


## Feature interactions

Mathematically you can include **interactions** offeatures

- An additional term that is the product of two or more features

$$\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_{12} x_1 x_2$$

- How much does $\hat y$ change if $x_1$ increases by one?
$$\frac{\partial \hat y}{\partial x_1} = b_1 + b_{12} x_2$$
- The effect of $x_1$ depends on the size of $x_2$

## Feature polynomials

You can interact a feature with itself

$$\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_{11} x_1 x_1$$
- How much does $\hat y$ change if $x_1$ increases by one?
$$\frac{\partial \hat y}{\partial x_1} = 2 b_1 x_1$$
- Creates a nonlinear effect
- The effect of a 1-unit increase in $x_1$ increases as $x_1$ increases


## Interactions in R Models

- Construct interaction features in R using the `*` operator
- R includes both the interaction and **the uninteracted features**
- e.g., `y ~ x1 * x2`
$$y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_{12} x_1 x_2$$

## Polynomials in R Models

- Construction polynomial interactions using the `*` operator
- R includes both the interaction and **uninteracted feature**
- e.g., `y ~ x1 * x1`
$$y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_{11} x_1 x_1$$


## Higher-order interactions

You can construct higher order interactions

- R includes all possible combinations of the individual features
- `y ~ x1*x2*x3`
$$\begin{aligned}
  y =& b_1 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_3 + \\
      & b_{12} x_1 x_2 + b_{13} x_1 x_3 + b_{23} x_2 x_3 + \\
      & b_{123} x_1 x_2 x_3
\end{aligned}$$

## Higher-order polynomials

You can construct higher order polynomials

- R includes all orders of polynomials up to the highest level
- `y ~ x1*x1*x1`
$$\begin{aligned}
  y =& b_1 + b_1 x_1 + b_{11} x_1 x_1 + b_{111} x_1 x_1 x_1
\end{aligned}$$

# Data: NOAA nClimDiv

## Data: NOAA nClimDiv

- NOAA's [US Climate Divisional Database](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/metadata/landing-page/bin/iso?id=gov.noaa.ncdc:C00005)
- Monthly, county-level climate data from 1895 to the present
- Temperature (min, max, average)
- Precipitation
- Heating and Cooling [Degree Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_day)

## Data: NOAA nClimDiv {.smaller}

Files in `Data/NOAA-NClimDiv`

Columns:

- **StateCountyFIPS**: State and County [FIPS Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIPS_county_code) 
- **Element**: Numeric code for the measurement
- **Year**: Numeric Year
- **Variable**: Alphabetic code for the measurement
- **Month**: Three-character month abbreviation 
- **Value**: Measured Value


## Example:PG's County July Temperatures {.smaller}

Let's look at Prince George's County (FIPS 26033) Temperatures 

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
read_parquet(file.path(data_path,"NOAA-NClimDiv","parquet","tmax.parquet")) |>
  filter(StateCountyFIPS == "26033") |>
  filter(Month == "Jul") |>
  select(Year,Value) |>
  rename(high_temp = Value) -> tmax

read_parquet(file.path(data_path,"NOAA-NClimDiv","parquet","tmin.parquet")) |>
  filter(StateCountyFIPS == "26033") |>
  filter(Month == "Jul") |>
  select(Year,Value) |>
  rename(low_temp = Value) -> tmin

tmax |>
  full_join(tmin,join_by(Year)) -> temps

ggplot(data=temps,mapping=aes(x=Year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y=high_temp,color="High"),linewidth=1.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y=low_temp,color="Low"),linewidth=1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("High"="red","Low"="blue")) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title="July Temperatures",
    subtitle="Prince George's County, MD",
    x="Year",
    y="Temperature (F)",
    color=""
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
All of the R code here should make sense, even without comments
